analysis.title: Consumer Health Check: Are higher prices finally catching up to consumers?
key_insights: Seasonally adjusted total card spending rose 5.6% YoY in October 2026 and 4.5% excluding gasoline. Momentum has moderated: card spending ex-gas grew at a 3.8% annualized pace over the past three months, barely keeping pace with inflation.

Spending has been resilient in 2026 despite rapid gasoline price increases, affordability concerns, above-trend inflation and higher interest rates. PNC attributes this to healthy household balance sheets entering the year and larger spring tax refunds.

PNC calls the evidence on whether higher prices are catching up with consumers mixed. Inflation-adjusted checking and savings balances remain elevated, median savings buffers are stable, and the share of households living paycheck-to-paycheck has not risen in 2026.

Households are leaning more on credit cards. Credit card balances per active account rose more than 9% YoY (9.4% as of September 2026), the fastest pace since before the pandemic, and the share of balances paid off each month has declined steadily through 2026. Balances per active account remain low.

Spending mix shows inflation fatigue. Gasoline is a growing share of card spend, while spending growth at discount retailers and wholesale clubs has accelerated markedly. General merchandise stores were +9.0% YoY in October and health and personal care +8.2%.
The K-shaped income divide reversed in 2026. Lower-income household spending growth has improved considerably and is closing the gap with upper-income households after stagnating over 2023-2025.

The divide is now generational. Boomers benefit from large post-pandemic net worth gains, cash savings well above pre-pandemic levels and less debt. Savings buffers for Gen Z, Millennials and Gen X have fallen much further.

Net inflows from investment and brokerage accounts into checking equal roughly 12% of Boomer card spending, more than twice the 2019 share. This gives Boomers extra liquidity after the equity market rally.

Gambling spend rose about 18% over the past year through October, but the growth comes from intensity, not participation. The share of households gambling was 7.3% in Jan-Oct 2026 vs 7.0% in 2023, while monthly transactions per active household rose roughly 70% since 2023 and average transaction size rose only about 5%.
The top 10% of gambling households account for more than 90% of total gambling spending and more than 90% of the increase over the past year. Their median spending has more than doubled since 2023.

High gambling spenders do not appear to be cutting other categories to fund gambling. Travel medians in the top gambling quartile were 7%-19% higher than the third quartile for Gen Z, Millennials and Gen X, and dining was slightly higher. Grocery and general merchandise were lower in all four generations.

Gas station card spend was up 22.8% YoY in October after 21.4% in September and 25.2% in May. Electronics and appliances were +12.7% and autos +6.8%. Food/beverage stores were -0.8% and non-store retailers -0.1%.

Conclusion: spending has moderated in late 2026 but remains healthy overall. Older and wealthier households are better positioned to absorb higher prices and rates, while younger households have smaller savings buffers and rely more on credit.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Strong on a year-ago basis, but momentum has moderated from the mid-year pace.
Underlying spending outside fuel is growing more slowly than the headline.
Barely keeps pace with inflation, so real spending growth is close to flat.

macro_indicators.indicator: Credit card balances per active account YoY
macro_indicators.interpretation: Fastest pace since before the pandemic, a sign households are borrowing more to sustain spending. Balance levels remain low.
One of the fastest-growing discretionary categories, driven by heavier use among a small group of households.

macro_indicators.indicator: Share of households with gambling spend
macro_indicators.interpretation: Participation is up little from 7.0% in 2023, so growth is not from broader participation.

risk_factors: Rapid gasoline price increases, ongoing affordability concerns, above-trend inflation and higher interest rates weigh on household budgets.
The boost from higher spring tax refunds has faded, removing a support for spending.
Rising credit card reliance and a falling share of balances paid off each month could strain younger households.
Younger households have much smaller savings buffers than Boomers and less room to absorb higher prices and rates.
Gambling growth is concentrated in a small group of heavy users, so aggregate gambling spend depends on a narrow base.

tension_points.bull_case: Household balance sheets remain very healthy. Inflation-adjusted checking and savings balances are elevated, median savings buffers are stable, and paycheck-to-paycheck share has not risen in 2026. Total card spend was +5.6% YoY in October.
tension_points.bear_case: Card spending ex-gas is growing at only 3.8% annualized over three months, credit card balances per active account are up more than 9% YoY, and the share of balances paid off monthly has declined through 2026.

tension_points.bull_case: Boomers hold elevated cash savings, carry less debt and receive investment inflows equal to roughly 12% of their card spending, so they can absorb higher prices and rates.
tension_points.bear_case: Younger household savings buffers have fallen much further, and these households rely more on credit.
